title: Hyundai Ioniq 6 Buying Guide: Cost, Reliability, and the Best Years to Own
summary: Our Hyundai Ioniq 6 buying guide covers the history and specs of the single model generation available, with advice on how much you can expect to pay for one, and which are the best and worst versions to buy.
body_markdown:
The Hyundai Ioniq 6 is a midsize electric sedan with a quirky fastback design and an interesting mix of mainstream affordability and available premium features. Introduced for the 2023 model year, its direct competitors include the BMW i4, the[Tesla Model 3](https://www.cargurus.com/research/articles/tesla-model-3-buying-guide) , and the Polestar 2, as well as the related Hyundai Ioniq 5 and Kia EV6. Because the Ioniq 6 is a sedan, it has a higher rate of depreciation than its crossover counterparts, which can make it a really good used buy.


At the time the Ioniq 6 was launched, it stood out as a non-luxury vehicle that offered more than 300 miles of all-electric range and ultra-fast charging. The single model generation available has a generally good reliability record, but one thing to watch out for with used models is an Integrated Charging Control Unit (ICCU) failure that’s covered by a recall that applies to all three model years.


As competitive as the Ioniq 6 was, it was discontinued in the U.S. after the 2025 model year. An updated version was launched in other markets for 2026, with the range including a new, high-performance Ioniq 6 N model featuring similar upgrades to the related Ioniq 5 N. At the time of writing, Hyundai said the Ioniq 6 N would be available in limited numbers in the U.S. from 2026, but hadn’t confirmed an on-sale date.


Our Hyundai Ioniq 6 buying guide covers the history and specs of the single model generation available to date, with advice on how much shoppers can expect to pay for one and which are the best and worst versions to buy.

# Hyundai Ioniq 6 Buying Guide: Cost, Reliability, and the Best Years to Buy

## Frequently Asked Questions


**Which Hyundai Ioniq 6 years are the best?**
With just three model years to choose from, we'd steer buyers toward the final year of U.S. sales—2025. Owner satisfaction is high for all three model years, and consumer complaints are fairly low. But 2025 gets Consumer Reports’ highest predictive reliability score and it's also the year with the fewest recalls and complaints logged on the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) website. In addition to having worked out early software bugs, a 2025 Ioniq 6 should still be covered by most of Hyundai’s original warranty.


**Which Hyundai Ioniq 6 years are the worst?**
We don’t think shoppers can really go wrong with any year of the Hyundai Ioniq 6, but the initial 2023 model year is the worst for problems, as is to be expected of a comparatively new model. This is the year that has the most consumer complaints, according to the NHTSA website, and it gets one of the lower predictive reliability scores from Consumer Reports. This model year also had some infotainment glitches on early builds and, as with other model years, is subject to the ICCU failure recall.


**Is a used Hyundai Ioniq 6 a good deal?**
On price alone, a used Hyundai Ioniq 6 is a very good deal considering the original prices ranged between $40,000 and $54,000. According to **[CarGurus pricing data](https://www.cargurus.com/research/price-trends/Hyundai-Ioniq-6-d3297)** , the average used price is now about $27,000. That means it's possible to buy a nearly new vehicle with modern tech, fast charging times, and excellent interior space for 30% to 50% off the original MSRP.

## Hyundai Ioniq 6 Generations


## Hyundai Ioniq 6 First Generation (2023-2025)


When the Hyundai Ioniq 6 launched in North America as a 2023 model, it became the second vehicle in Hyundai’s Ioniq EV sub-brand. Underneath, it used the same basic platform as the Hyundai Ioniq 5 and the Kia EV6. It had a range of up to 361 miles at launch which, at the time, was one of the longest EPA-estimated maximum ranges available from a non-luxury automaker.


At launch, the Ioniq 6 offered two battery packs: 53 kWh and 77.4 kWh. The base model with the smaller battery pack had rear-wheel drive (RWD) and delivered 149 horsepower. The larger battery could be paired with either rear-wheel drive or all-wheel drive (AWD), delivering 225 hp and 320 hp respectively. The smaller battery pack offered up to 240 miles of range, while the Long Range model gave 361 miles with RWD and 316 miles with AWD.


Throughout its three-year lifespan, the Ioniq 6 had three trims: SE, SEL, and Limited. Only the base SE was available with the smaller battery pack and, when equipped with the larger battery pack, all trims were available with either RWD or AWD.


With the standard battery, base SE trim included 18-inch alloy wheels, LED headlights and taillights, heated power side mirrors, heated front seats, a power-adjustable driver’s seat, dual-zone automatic climate control, ambient lighting, dual 12.3-inch display screens, wired Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, navigation, and a six-speaker audio system. Upgrading to the Long Range battery options on the SE trim added a heat pump, battery pre-conditioning, and a vehicle-to-load (V2L) capability that allowed buyers to power electric devices using the car’s battery pack.


SEL and Limited trims added more standard features. For example, SEL added 20-inch wheels, leatherette seating surfaces, a 64-color ambient lighting system, a smart key, and enhanced adaptive cruise control. Limited trim was the luxury option, including features such as a power sunroof, automatic wipers, power-folding side mirrors, ventilated front seats, a heated steering wheel, a power-adjustable passenger seat, rear sunshades, a surround-view camera system, a Bose premium audio system, a blind-spot monitor, an interior V2L outlet in the back seat, and remote smart park assist.


Since this single model generation only spans three years, changes for each year are relatively minor. They boil down to some packaging and trim adjustments, such as adding a head-up display to the Limited trim in 2025.


From the get-go, the Ioniq 6 included a lot of standard safety features, including automatic emergency braking, blind-spot monitors, rear cross-traffic alert, lane-keep assist, adaptive cruise control, safe-exit warning, front and rear parking sensors, high-beam assist, and a rear-occupant alert system. Available features included blind-spot collision avoidance, a blind-spot monitor display, automatic reverse braking, and remote smart park assist. It is no surprise, then, that every model year gets an Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) Top Safety Pick+ designation and a five-out-of-five overall rating from the NHTSA.


Several of the known issues are the subject of recalls, and that includes the ICCU failures, seat-belt anchors that may detach in a crash, and charging port doors that may come off while driving. These three recalls affect all model years. Ensuring that these recalls have been properly completed is key when buying used, and can be done via a VIN check. With regard to the ICCU failures, it’s worth noting that there is a small subset of owners reporting a repeat failure after at least one repair.


Another recall affects only 2024 model year cars and concerns differential gear bolts that may not have been correctly tightened. Other reported faults include infotainment freezes, navigation glitches, charging schedule problems, and similar software bugs. These primarily affect 2023 and some early 2024 models.


According to **[CarGurus pricing data](https://www.cargurus.com/research/price-trends/Hyundai-Ioniq-6-d3297)** , the average price of a used Hyundai Ioniq 6 is about $27,000. Both the 2023 and 2024 models have an average transaction price of $26,000, while 2025 models have an average price of around $31,000.
